claim: Charles Ponzi promised clients a 50% profit within 45 days or 100% profit within 90 days.
excerpt: He promised clients a 50% profit within 45 days or 100% profit within 90 days

claim: The scheme claimed to profit by buying discounted postal reply coupons abroad and redeeming them at face value in the U.S.
excerpt: buying discounted postal reply coupons in other countries and redeeming them at face value in the U.S.

claim: Financial journalist Clarence Barron noted that 160 million coupons would have to be in circulation to cover the investments, while only about 27,000 actually were.
excerpt: 160 million postal reply coupons would have to be in circulation. However, only about 27,000 actually were.

claim: On 26 July 1920 the Boston Post began articles asking hard questions; the articles caused a run on the company, and Ponzi paid out $2 million in three days to a crowd outside his office.
excerpt: Ponzi paid out $2 million in three days to a wild crowd outside his office.
context: The Post series began 26 July 1920 (stated in the article).

claim: On 11 August 1920 the Bank Commissioner seized Hanover Trust; the news brought down five other banks, and investors lost about $20 million in 1920 dollars, receiving less than 30 cents on the dollar.
excerpt: They lost about $20 million in 1920 dollars

claim: Ponzi was charged with 86 counts of mail fraud, pleaded guilty on 1 November 1920 to a single count, and was sentenced to five years in federal prison.
excerpt: Ponzi was charged with 86 counts of mail fraud
context: The guilty plea and the sentence are in the same paragraph of the article.

claim: Ponzi was released in 1934 and deported to Italy on 7 October.
excerpt: On 7 October, Ponzi was officially deported.

claim: He died in the charity ward of a hospital in Rio de Janeiro on 18 January 1949, leaving an estate of $75.
excerpt: He left an estate of $75, which was barely enough to bury him.
